message.content:
Yes.
The answer is yes.
Discrete random variables can have finite means.
Their sum may fail to have a finite expectation.
This happens when positive and negative parts are not integrable together.
The definition of expectation for an integer valued variable uses a signed sum.
If the sum of positive terms and negative terms both diverge, the total is undefined.
The variables can still have finite individual expectations.
A finite mean requires the positive part and negative part to have finite values.
The sum X plus Y can mix tails in a more complicated way.
It can create cancellation that is not valid under improper summation.
Countable probability spaces simplify the construction for discrete variables.
We can assign probabilities to countably many outcomes.
Each variable can be defined on the same space.
Each variable can be assigned values that make its own expectation finite.
The joint distribution controls the behavior of the sum.
By choosing paired values carefully, one can force the sum to have heavy tails.
The positive part of X plus Y may diverge.
The negative part of X plus Y may also diverge.
Then the expectation of X plus Y is not defined.
This is a classic subtlety in probability theory.
It shows that linearity of expectation needs an integrability condition.
Consider a special case where two distinct discrete random variables have finite expectations but their combined expectation is not defined because the positive and negative tails can interfere in a very delicate way beneath the surface.
